ety.text: From Middle English myself, meself, from Old English mē selfum and similar phrases, equivalent to me + self, later partly reinterpreted as my + self / -self. Cognate with Scots mysel, mysell (“myself”), West Frisian mysels (“myself”), Dutch mijzelf (“myself”), German mich selbst, mir selbst (“myself”), Norwegian Bokmål meg selv (“myself”).

senses.d: Me, as direct or indirect object the speaker as the object of a verb or preposition, when the speaker is also the subject.
ex: I taught myself.
(I) don’t think much of your new car, myself.

senses.d: Personally, for my part; used in apposition to I, sometimes for simple emphasis and sometimes with implicit exclusion of any others performing the activity described.
ex: I myself have witnessed the event.

senses.d: In my normal state of body or mind.
ex: I feel like myself.

senses.d: Me, as the object of a verb or preposition without a reflexive trigger. Sometimes used for intensifying the pronoun of oneself.
ex: Give the ball to John or myself.

senses.d: I (as the subject of a verb).
ex: My wife and myself want to go on vacation.
Myself am confident that an ointment of it is one of the best remedies for a scabby head that is.

senses.d: my name is...
ex: Myself John.

ety.text: From Middle English mysterie, from Anglo-Norman misterie (Old French mistere), from Latin mysterium, from Ancient Greek μυστήριον (mustḗrion, “a mystery, a secret, a secret rite”), from μύστης (mústēs, “initiated one”), from μυέω (muéō, “to initiate”), from μύω (múō, “to shut”). Displaced native Old English ġerȳne.

senses.d: Something secret or unexplainable; an unknown.
ex: The truth behind the events remains a mystery.

senses.d: Someone or something with an obscure or puzzling nature.
ex: That man is a mystery.

senses.d: An account, story, book, film, or play, often with the theme of crime or murder, with a surprise ending that explains all the strange events that have occurred.
A mystery play.
A secret or mystical meaning.
ex: […] and, not knowing the meaning or misterie of her pollicie, forgat no termes of reproche or rigorous rebuke against his chast doughter.

senses.d: A religious truth not understandable by the application of human reason alone (without divine aid).
A sacrament.
A secret religious celebration, admission to which was usually through initiation.
ex: the Eleusinian mysteries
the Mysteries of Mithras

senses.d: A particular event or series of events in the life of Christ.
ex: The second decade of the Rosary concerns the Sorrowful mysteries, such as the crucifixion and the crowning with thorns.

senses.d: A craft, art or trade; specifically a guild of craftsmen.
ex: The trades, the crafts, the mysteries, would all be losers.
